speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: asked the Minister for Education what are the Ministry’s plans to seamlessly execute COVID-19 vaccination for Primary school children without disrupting national examinations, school examinations, co-curricular activities and other classroom time and attendance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have seen an encouraging start to the vaccination exercise for our children.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will continue to work with our parents to achieve a high vaccination rate so that it would be possible to resume as many school activities as possible in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The pace, extent and approach towards resuming these school activities would depend on various factors, including vaccination rates as well as the overall national posture.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Schools will help students catch up on missed lessons and work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We strongly encourage parents to get their child vaccinated as early as possible to keep our children, families and the wider community safe and resilient against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first pertains to a subject I believe that was covered both by the Minister for Health and the Minister for Education.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This concerns the apprehension some parents have over the administration of mRNA vaccines for their children.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These parents anecdotally are not anti-vax per se.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some of them may have taken the mRNA vaccine on their own, but the concern is really a visceral one, that is, about the long-term effects, the fact that this vaccine is referred for emergency approvals and so forth, even though I think some have been granted FDA approval, Pfizer-BioNTech specifically.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand that one such non-mRNA vaccine company, Novavax, submitted data for approval under Singapore's Pandemic Special Access Route (PSAR) on 22 November.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Director of Medical Services confirmed a few days ago, on 5 January, that he was very optimistic Novavax would be authorised as a non-mRNA booster.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My question is, if Novavax or any other non-mRNA vaccine maker has submitted data for the authorisation for use for children above the age of 12, and, if so, when can these vaccines be expected to be introduced in the National Vaccination Programme?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just a very short follow-through on that: with regard to the point made by the Minister for Health on the 270 days that are required, the limit before you take a booster and then to be recognised still as being vaccinated, would there be some flexibility to allow Novavax at least to get on this programme and to allow more individuals to then be considered fully vaccinated?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I can fully appreciate parents' concern about mRNA vaccines for children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They will be concerned about the long-term effects and whatever side effects there may be.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The children's vaccine, Pfizer-BioNTech/Comirnaty, has gone through extensive clinical trials.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And during the clinical trials, it was proven and shown to be safe and effective.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Specifically, myocarditis, which is what most parents are concerned about in children, it occurred.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And as Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary mentioned, we have to balance this against the downside of getting infection.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we have seen a handful, one or two a week, when Delta was at its peak and they are admitted to ICU.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, there is a good track record of safety and efficacy for the children's vaccine.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the other hand, for children who are infected with COVID-19, while, generally, children are more resilient, we have seen cases of myocarditis and MIS-C.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do have to weigh those costs and benefits.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do have to add one more fact, which is that, for the children's vaccine, it is a diluted form.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are not taking the same adult vaccine.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, these are the facts and parents will have to make the right decision.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As of now, we are quite encouraged that many parents are coming forward and the paediatric vaccination exercise is actually gathering pace, and many parents are coming forward to protect their children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to let the scientists do their work.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think we should consider putting it into our National Vaccination Programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have always wanted a good portfolio of mRNA and non-mRNA vaccines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, as for the timing, I think it may take a while more, including for delivery, plus another process for assessing whether it is suitable for children, there is another set of data, another set of trials.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I do not know how long it would take.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the meantime, Omicron is upon us, highly transmissible, and we do not want to rule out that even a small percentage of children can get very sick; we might be looking at a significant absolute number.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I would suggest, as Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary has advised, get your child vaccinated with mRNA, given the circumstances.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not perfect, but I think, given the circumstances, cause and benefits, the right thing to do now is to get your child vaccinated as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While I hope we have the luxury of time to wait for a non-mRNA vaccine to be available, but, with the impending Omicron wave, I think we should act quickly and, therefore, we set the validity period of 270 days.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My supplementary question is for Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some young children may have undetected medical conditions and, especially allergies, if their parents do not send them for non-mandatory medical reviews.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, I wish to ask whether MOH would advise all young children to undergo a medical review before going ahead with the COVID-19 vaccination.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is similar to how some adults with underlying medical conditions are advised to get clearance from the doctor in the early stages of the vaccination drive.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The answer is partly in the last line that he stated, which is, that we took that approach in the early stages of the adult vaccination drive because, at that time, the amount of data that we had was less and the amount of experience that we had was less.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Now we know a lot more about both the disease as well as the vaccination, including in children.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the approach for children is not so different from adults.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If they have an underlying condition – and there is a list that the doctor will know about it – then some review needs to happen.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But if the child is otherwise healthy, then the recommendation is to proceed with the COVID-19 vaccination.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue of allergies is slightly different in that, for any drug, you cannot necessarily tell whether an allergy will happen or not happen on the basis of prior underlying conditions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Hence, the team at the site of the vaccination is trained to then detect and deal with the rare allergies that do happen.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And again, our experience with COVID-19 is, it does not happen any differently from other vaccinations that we are giving to children on a regular basis.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the short answer to the Member's question whether all children should go for medical review prior to COVID-19 is "no".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government has been encouraging the use of ART swabbing to prevent the spread of viruses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, in many situations, self-reporting of ART results is not allowed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Instead, people are required to conduct the test only at approved testing centres, which not only costs more but is more inconvenient.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can we move to a regime where people are trusted to accurately report the ART results, just like how it is done in schools and, indeed, here in Parliament?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will reduce the cost for many people and make administrative procedures at events more efficient.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second question: there is a tendency for some activities to be prohibited, even though the transmission risk is low.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the lead agencies issue more specific advisories to organisations based on the actual prevailing risk of viral spread, so that we move closer on the path towards normalcy?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not quite in Parliament because you do get informed by an SMS that you are negative.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But there are many settings where we do rely on self-reporting.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Workplace, for example, a lot of meetings, events you go to, you do a self-test.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have an entire protocol, what we call a protocol tool, that is based on self-testing – that you self-test and, if you are positive, you stay home for 72 hours.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: After that, daily tests and only when you are negative, you come out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You will notice that, recently, MOH announced that we are now working with general practitioners (GPs) and primary care-providers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I must say that, to overcome this crisis, it is really not just the Government, but it requires the cooperation, civic-mindedness and sense of self-responsibility of every individual in our population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The next question is more specific: rules on different settings.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is what we have been doing, too.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the Member has any specific suggestion on specific settings, we would be happy to hear them and we are constantly tweaking them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Sometimes, when you tweak more, it becomes more complicated and people do compare: "Why is it for this setting I am allowed to do this?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Why is it for that setting I am not allowed?" And you start to have invidious comparisons and people start to get confused.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we are also very mindful to keep rules as simple as possible because simplicity is an essential ingredient for people to exercise self-responsibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What they do not understand, they cannot self-enforce.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: One is regarding a question that I raised in my Parliamentary Question (PQ), which is yet to be answered.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: With quite a significant proportion of Omicron coming from imported cases, I had asked the Minister for a breakdown by country of origin of imported COVID-19 Omicron cases.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, if the Minister for Health could shed some light on that.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: My second question relates to his answer that boosters have shown to increase protection against infection and severe illness, including Omicron, substantially; whether MOH will contemplate imposition of booster jab as a requirement for VTL travellers, beyond the current requirement of two jabs only and that would be deemed as vaccinated.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, whether we will bump up the requirement to a booster jab.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I did not mean to drop her question but it will be addressed by Minister Iswaran later in the next set of questions, especially on the specific breakdown on the number of imported cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for booster jabs, it is a serious issue that the Member has raised because we do know that two doses do not last forever.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think the world will converge towards some form of validity, I believe, and, naturally, this will become a requirement in due course.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I just have one supplementary question for the Minister for Education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My question, however, is whether there should be activities beyond school, perhaps, say, if and when the National School Games should commence or if there are national-level sporting or athletic activities that will involve children aged five to 11, would there be possibly vaccination-differentiated measures implemented then.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, would there be a position that might say if young children are not vaccinated or not fully vaccinated, they would not be allowed to participate in these events?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I ask also primarily because, sometimes, the results of these events for the children – the timings, their performances and so on, especially for those in Primary 6 this year – could be relevant and important in the application for secondary schools under Direct School Admission (DSA).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Of course, I caveat that by saying that whatever our considerations current at this point in time will, subsequently, have to take into account the prevailing national posture and also the development of the virus and its mutation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At this point in time, we would very much like to have all our children be able to attend school and participate in as many of the core activities as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having said that, of course, there are also activities beyond the core curriculum that may pose a higher risk to our students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And for those higher-risk activities, we will then have to consider if differentiated measures will be required.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, at this point in time, we have already put in place some additional measures for some of these activities that the students are participating in, and these apply to our secondary, Junior College (JC) and Millenia Institute (MI) students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For some other students who are participating in the band or the choir, they would also have to take some other additional measures to safeguard themselves and their fellow participants.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, this is how we will go about considering the participation of our students in some of these particularly higher-risk activities in the sense that they have a higher-risk of transmission.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But as far as possible, we would like to have our students participate in the core curriculum all together because this adds to their overall social emotional development beyond their academic development.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I just have one supplementary question which is, essentially, the PQ that I asked.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do understand the need to be nimble.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But, basically, having that decision-making framework and matrix published would actually help businesses and consumers to have greater confidence and clarity and, certainly, better than the situation where some people feel a certain sense of nervousness whenever the Multi-Ministry Task Force (MTF) holds a press conference, especially those in F&B businesses which are most affected by the dine-in rules.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Member reiterated his question, but I may have to reiterate my answer.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think there are so many twists and turns in this pandemic, we would rather be a bit more nimble and to be able to adapt.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we take the Member's point, and we have always adopted this position that we do not go for "Freedom Day", neither do we go for zero COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We want to strike a balance, preserve the healthcare capacity; at the same time, allow people to live life as normally as possible, businesses to be able to operate and survive.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I also hope that, over time, people will begin to understand what our key considerations are, even though we may not be able to pinpoint trigger points.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should say that, ultimately, it is not about the numbers that cause all this uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a fact that we are in the middle of a pandemic and our society, for two years, we were not entirely ready in the first year in terms of our resilience.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Last year, we were much better, and I do believe that, in 2022, we will be even better and that is most important.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Remember, in 2020, when we faced a wave – it was hardly a wave, it was just clusters – we went into circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Last year, in 2021, when we faced a wave, we went into what we called "Phase Two (Heightened Alert)".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Restaurants did not close towards the end of the year, but they operated with dine-in group size of two.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hopefully, this year, we can ride through waves with a much more liberal posture and that is how we keep on improving.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And that is most important to our businesses.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I have two questions for the Minister for Health, and this is with regard to averting a testing crunch that we see around the world amidst an Omicron-driven wave.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My first question is, in the event of such a wave, how do we plan to avoid a run on testing facilities in our healthcare system for people who are keen to get a test – either PCR or ART – and this includes, of course, primary care providers that the Minister has mentioned in his answer, but also, importantly, emergency departments?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How do we avoid a run on healthcare facilities for people who are keen to get a test ordered?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the second question first, to keep prices steady and affordable, I think competition helps, choices help.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we are constantly on the lookout for kits that are effective as well as lower priced.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There have been many kits out there that claim to be cheaper but are not as effective.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, HSA does not approve all of them just unquestioningly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As to the Member's question on how to prevent a run on testing facilities, number one, is to try as much as possible to plan ahead, have supply agreements signed, stock up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we will continue to monitor the situation, bearing in mind that we have seen in other countries where there has been a run.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, to prevent a run, do not make people panic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Omicron can be scary, it can go up a few times, it can be 10,000 cases, 15,000 cases a day.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we have extended this now to GPs to also trigger Protocol 2.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That way, I think people are sensitised to "when I need a test, what do I do after a test?" And when people know what they need to do, they do not panic, there is much less chance of a run on any testing facility.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because there is a strong request from the parents that, at least, there should be more choices for vaccines and the VDS measures will not be applied to the children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also received feedback from residents that some teachers have already practised VDS measures in schools.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, can the Minister confirm whether the teachers are practising that or if any officers in the schools are practising that, that it is against the Government's policy at the moment?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I refer to the messages and then I give a reply later?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want, as far as possible, for our students to be able to participate in the core curriculum, in the school activities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For certain selected activities that may be deemed of higher risk, we may consider applying specific measures for them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I have raised two very specific examples.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One, for example, of students participating in the playing of wind instruments or the choir; and two, students participating in sports activities that may require physical contact or close physical contact.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I also caveated my explanation by saying that, of course, we will have to look at the overall national posture and how the virus will continue to evolve for us to adjust our policies accordingly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have a clarification for the Minister for Health regarding the COVID-19 statistics that he cited earlier and also, in general, statistics reported by the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have come across cases of individuals who did self-testing by ART and, they were positive.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But they did not report themselves to the authorities or to any clinics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With home recovery now as the default response to any positive COVID-19 test, does Minister agree that the risk of unreported cases is, actually, quite high?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And to that extent, we need to be quite careful when we look at the official statistics recorded by the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In every country, they also have a concept of what they call "ascertainment rate", which is, of the underlying cases, how many are uncovered and reported.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And every country knows that it cannot be 80%, 90% or 100%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Especially when you have a Delta wave or Omicron wave that is highly transmissible, you do want people to take self-responsibility, take care of themselves, isolate themselves and, in these cases, they may not be reported.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To think about it, when we face an endemic disease, whether it is chicken pox or influenza, we cannot report every case and that is what endemicity means, which is, many people get it, many people are able to recover without it being officially reported.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That will always give us a consistent measure of the prevalence of the virus in the community.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we will continue to do so in a practical way.
